Power cuts
Power cuts (or electricity outages) can have a number of causes including severe weather, which can lead to damaged infrastructure, or system faults.
The UK has a resilient electricity system. Most power cuts are short-lived and occur locally, but more widespread and longer outages can happen. These could potentially last several days with regional or, although unlikely, national impacts.
Gas ovens, boilers, heat pumps and your home internet won’t work without power. Your mobile phone might stop working if your local mast is in the affected area. Mains water supply to your home could also be disrupted during and after power cuts. Find out what to do in a phone and broadband outage, or a water outage.
Actions to take to prepare for a power cut
Keep a battery or wind-up torch (and spare batteries) at home. Torches are safer than candles. You probably won’t want to use the torch on your mobile phone as this will drain its batteries more quickly.
Keep at least 3 days’ worth of bottled water (3 litres per person per day) and non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables and a tin opener. You should also include ready-made baby formula and pet food if needed.
If you’re eligible, sign up to your energy supplier’s Priority Service Register to let them know that you need additional support during a power cut. Lots of households are eligible, including those with children under 5.
If you have solar panels and a battery storage system with power backup capability, some installations can continue to provide power during a power cut if they are designed and configured to operate independently of the electricity grid. This may help you keep essential appliances running during an outage.
Find out your power/load block letter. In the unlikely event of a national energy shortage, emergency power cuts could be scheduled on a rotating area-by-area basis. Each area in GB is assigned a ‘load block letter’ and would be scheduled to disconnect from the electricity grid for around three hours at a time. You can find which load block letter you are in by entering your postcode at powercut105.com, or some energy suppliers include it on electricity bills.
Keep a small amount of cash for essential purchases if electronic payments or ATMs are disrupted.
You would lose internet connection and possibly mobile signal during a power cut. To prepare for this:
Write down the phone number to report a power cut – this is 105 in England, Scotland and Wales and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland. You can also save the number in your mobile phone.
Keep a battery or wind-up radio (and spare batteries) at home. There might be updates communicated by radio during a power cut. A car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside. Write down on paper the frequencies of any local or national radio stations you use for news updates. You could add these to your household emergency plan.
It can be helpful to keep these notes with other items you might have, such as a torch or radio, and in a place that’s easy to find in the dark.
If your only way of making emergency calls is through a landline phone, or if you have a telecare kit connected to your landline, contact your landline provider to understand whether your phone will work during a power cut. If your landline will not work during a power cut, your landline provider might offer you a free solution (such as a back-up battery unit), for a minimum of one hour, that would enable you to call the emergency services during a power cut if you needed to.
If you have a personal alarm (also known as telecare devices) or other connected equipment monitoring your health such as diabetes sensors, speak to your device provider/manufacturer to understand how they will function during a power cut.
Actions to take during a power cut
Visit your local network operator’s website to report a power cut and track updates when there’s a problem. If you’re unable to report the power cut online, call 105 for free in England, Wales and Scotland and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland.
Keep away from hazards such as power lines. Electricity at high voltages can jump gaps with no warning.
Turn off items such as irons, ovens, electric fires and fryers. Unplug your TV and PC as they can be damaged if there is a surge when power goes back on.
Keep warm by using blankets and layered clothing. Keep doors of unused rooms closed and close curtains to keep the heat in. Older adults, babies and young children, and people with long-term health problems are most likely to become ill if they get too cold.
Check in on neighbours and, if you are able, offer to share blankets, clothing or other supplies such as food. You can also pass on any important information you might have received about the power cut, such as when the power is expected to go back on. If you have a corded landline phone, this might still be working in a power cut. The mobile phone network may still temporarily work in specific regions with backup power.
In a power cut your TV or internet might not be working. To get news updates use a battery or wind-up radio to search for stations that are still broadcasting. Try FM and digital modes. You can use the radio in your car, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside.
If you have a power cut and you don’t have back-up power to your landline phone (or have a corded landline) and have a life-threatening emergency, you should attempt to call 999 or 112 using a mobile. You might receive overlapping signal from a nearby area that is unaffected – emergency calls automatically ‘roam’ onto all available networks.
Keep fridges and freezer doors closed, as this will ensure they stay cold for several hours. The Food Standards Agency provides advice on food safety in a power cut and answers to come common food safety questions.
To prepare baby formula safely, you will need to be able to boil water and follow the normal safety procedures. If you have no tap water, using ready-made or ready-to-feed formula is the safest option. Powdered formula is not sterile and should only be prepared using freshly boiled water. Bottled water is not usually recommended for making up formula milk feeds. This is because it’s not sterile and may contain too much salt (sodium) or sulphate. But in rare circumstances, such as when drinking water is unavailable or has been contaminated, you can use still bottled water to make up formula feeds. Check the label to ensure it does not have more than 200 mg per litre (mg/L) of sodium or 250 mg/L of sulphate. It should be boiled (to sterilise) and allowed to cool for no more than 30 minutes. The NHS provides advice on making up baby formula.
Available support for those with additional needs
If you use medical equipment that requires a power supply, make a plan with your care provider and/or clinical care teams now about what will happen in a power cut. The plan should set out what action you, or someone you care for, needs to take and who to contact if there’s a power outage. Ensure that your care provider, clinical care team and/or equipment supplier has supplied you with enough information so that you understand how the equipment works and what to do if there is a power disruption.
The energy networks can help if you have additional needs because of your medical or personal circumstances. The Priority Services Register (available to customers in England and Wales, and in Scotland), is a free service to help people who have additional needs. You can sign up by using the link above or by contacting your energy supplier. If you are in Northern Ireland these are called Customer Care Registers. Wherever possible, you will receive advanced notice of scheduled power cuts. If you rely on your energy supply for medical reasons, your network operator can tell you about planned power cuts, for example, when they plan engineering work. You can also get priority support in an emergency.

Be ready for emergencies
Here are some simple and effective steps you can take to be ready for emergencies and the disruption they cause. Many of these activities can be helpful across a range of different types of emergency. You can also download the Be Ready checklist .
There are lots of suggestions here that won’t cost anything and just take a few minutes to do.
For various reasons, not everyone will be able to take all the actions in the guidance and some people will only follow a few of the recommended steps. The details below provide basic advice on how to prepare, so you can take the steps that work for you.
Community groups and volunteers plan and prepare for emergencies, often working with emergency responders to get help to those who need it most.
Call 999 if you or someone else is in immediate danger
Be Ready checklist
Being ready for 3 days helps you manage while support reaches those most in need.
Doing this is easier than you might think. You could have some of the items at home already.
You don’t need to do it all at once. Build up your readiness gradually over time by taking it step by step, and picking up an extra item or two when you can.
How to get started:
See what you already have: Check your cupboards first to see what essentials you already keep at home.
Plan for your household: Note down what you still need, remembering items your family relies on, such as medical supplies, baby formula or pet food.
Build it gradually: Pick up missing items when you can during your regular shopping trips to help spread the cost.
Check it regularly: Set a reminder every six months to check expiry dates and swap out items that need replacing, or update your kit if your household’s needs have changed.
Connect with your community: Talk to your neighbours about what extra support you might be able to share during an outage, and swap contact details.
Use the checklist below to see what you have and consider anything else you might need.
CategoryItems to check off
Water☐ Bottled water for 3 days
3 litres per person per day for drinking. More would be needed for other tasks such as cooking and washing.
Food☐ Non-perishable food for 3 days
Food with a long shelf life that doesn’t need refrigeration or cooking e.g. tinned meat, fish or vegetables, dried fruit and nuts. It’s best to buy food you’d usually eat.
Hygiene☐ Hand sanitiser, wet wipes and bathroom products
Light and warmth☐ Torch (and spare batteries)
Torches are safer than candles.
☐ Blankets, sleeping bags and warm clothing
Homes can become cold very quickly when the heating goes off.
Communication and information☐ FM radio (battery / wind up)
For updates during outages, write down frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.
☐ Charged power bank
To charge phones or compatible medical devices.
Money and documents☐ Cash (mix of coins and notes) and cards
In case electronic payments or ATMs are disrupted. The amount of cash you should keep depends on your family’s specific needs for essentials.
☐ Copies of IDs / documents
Have printed copies of important documents such as passports, birth certificates, insurance policy details and instructions for any medical equipment you rely on.
☐ Important phone numbers and information
Write down contact details of who you’d need to contact in an emergency (including anyone who might need checking on) and a list of any regular medication and doses.
Medical and health☐ First aid kit / first aid items
Including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.
☐ Essential medication and medical supplies
Always leave enough time to request repeat prescriptions so you have less chance of running out in an emergency. It’s important to request prescriptions up to 5 working days before you need your medicine.
Baby products☐ Baby formula
Ready-made or ‘ready-to-feed’ formula is best, as you may not be able to boil water to make up powdered formula safely.
☐ Nappies and wipes
Pet products☐ Pet food and bottled water
If you have any extra items, you could consider donating these to others who might not have the means to prepare their own households. You may be able to help someone by photocopying or printing important documents for them.
Be informed
Sign up for alerts and warnings and find out about different types of hazards and emergencies.
Find out more about risks in your local area including checking your flood risk for areas in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Learn some basic first aid skills. Check online to find free workshops or ask if your employer will pay for a course.
Check if the place where you work or volunteer has a plan for what you should do if you cannot contact them during an emergency, for example in a power cut.
Find out if you are eligible to sign up to the Priority Services Register (PSR)
Visit thepsr.co.uk to find out if you are eligible and sign up to the Priority Service Register – this lets your electricity, gas and water providers know that you need additional support, including when there is an interruption to your supply. Lots of households are eligible, including those with children under 5.
This service is available to customers in England, Scotland and Wales – if you are in Northern Ireland these are called Customer Care Registers.
Make a plan
Use our downloadable and printable household emergency plan. You could keep this with other important documents such as passports, birth certificates and insurance policies so it’s easier to gather them quickly if needed.
Work out the best escape route from your home if there is a fire or what you should do if your home floods – if you live with others, including children, discuss this with them.
Decide on a meeting point with family members in case you cannot return home or contact each other for a period of time. Choose places that are easy to find and open to the public in your community, or you might agree to meet at a family member’s home if it is safe to do so.
Agree on a backup plan with anyone who might need extra support, particularly if they live alone. You could agree that if an outage happens and you cannot call, you or another trusted person they know will visit them in person. Remind them that they should follow the advice of the emergency services if they are asked to evacuate for their safety.
You can also speak to the neighbours of anyone you would be worried about in an outage and agree that they will check on them.
Write down important phone numbers on paper and store them somewhere easy to find in a power cut. Include the phone number to report a power cut (105 in England, Scotland and Wales and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland), phone numbers of anyone you would want to contact in an emergency, a list of your regular medication, frequencies of radio stations you use for news updates, and insurance policy details.
Add emergency contacts or medical information to your mobile phone (often called ‘ICE’ or ‘Medical ID’ on smartphones) so that emergency services can access this information without having to unlock your phone with a passcode – consider the sensitivity of the information you are including (anyone could see it who has access to your mobile phone) and let the person you’ve selected as your emergency contact know.
Check your child’s school (or other childcare provider) has the correct contact numbers for you in case they need to contact you during an emergency. Your child’s school should have plans and procedures in place to deal with different types of emergencies, for example for severe weather, loss of utilities and fire.
Prepare your home
Complete an online home fire safety check to help keep you and your home safe from fire.
Set a reminder in your phone or make a note on your calendar to check your smoke alarms at least once a month – the Fire Kills campaign website has advice on fire safety in the home.
Know how to turn off your gas, electricity and water – you’ll need to turn these off if you have to leave your home due to flooding or for other reasons such as if there’s a leak.
Check the right insurance is in place for your home (or business), for example, flood insurance.
If you live in a flood risk area, find out more actions you can take to prepare your property.
You could consider keeping some essential items you might need to take with you if asked to leave your home quickly in a spare bag – you might hear some people call this a ‘grab bag’.
Have a look at the hot weather, cold weather and storms pages for more advice on how you can prepare your property.
Pack a few essential items in your car boot to make sure you’re ready in case of getting stuck in wintry weather – this can include a torch, in-car phone charger, warm clothes and blankets, high-visibility clothing, jump leads, food and drink, and a shovel for snow. It can also be helpful to keep a first aid kit in your car.
Talk to others
Talk about the advice on this website and pass on information about the support available – help your friends, family, neighbours and colleagues to undertake the simple actions on this website, if they can.
Swap contact details with neighbours and consider creating an instant messaging group or other closed online social network for your street or building – these can be an important source of information and support during an emergency.
Ask your neighbours if they might have additional support needs during an emergency – they may have additional medical needs, be new to the area, are not able to use the internet or technology well, or not speak or read English well. Talk to them about the help available and how you can support them.
Make a plan to check in on neighbours if an emergency happens, particularly if the power goes out.
Talk to children about what to do in an emergency, including how and when to call the emergency services – the Staywise website includes information and resources on emergencies aimed at children. You can also help them to learn their home address and if possible, a parent/guardian’s mobile phone number – practise these regularly.

News story
Households encouraged to take small, simple steps to stay prepared in an emergency
Households are being encouraged to take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted, under updated advice published today.
From:
Cabinet Office and The Rt Hon Dan Jarvis MBE MP
Published:
22 October 2026
Advice helps people feel better prepared for events such as severe weather, which can occasionally affect services like power, water, and the internet.
Campaign bolsters UK’s preparedness for emergencies, in line with European peers including France, Ireland and The Netherlands.
Simple steps include actions that are completely free, like signing up to the Priority Services Register, a service helping utility companies identify people most in need.
Households are being encouraged to take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted, under updated advice published today.
The advice is the first stage of a three-year campaign to help households across the UK feel better prepared for events such as severe weather, which can occasionally affect services including power, water, phones and the internet.
The campaign focuses on straightforward things people can do in advance, including signing up to the Priority Services Register - a service that helps gas, water, and electricity companies identify customers that may need extra support in an emergency - and keep a small supply of non-perishable food and bottled water at home.
With storms last winter and the wildfires this summer showing how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, from phone signal to water and the internet, launching the campaign brings the UK into line with European peers who all run similar campaigns already.
The government has worked with other countries to learn from their experience and best practice. For example, the advice to be prepared for three days of disruption that is at the heart of the UK campaign is also used by France, Ireland and The Netherlands.
The government has also worked closely with local resilience forums across the UK to root the advice in what works for local communities.
Dan Jarvis MP, Security Minister, said:
Those who can follow this advice should follow this advice. By taking simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies like severe storms, people can reduce pressure on emergency services, helping them prioritise people who need more support in an emergency.
This is just the sort of community-focused campaign the UK needs to improve our resilience as a nation. It will bring us into line with European counterparts, where advice like this is a normal part of everyday life.
The ‘Be Ready’ campaign will build gradually over time. More than five hundred organisations across the UK, from charities to businesses, have already signed-up to share messaging and campaign assets within their networks and communities. Government channels like GOV.UK and social media accounts will also amplify content.
Over the coming weeks and months, social media and radio advertising will help reach audiences who may be particularly at-risk in everyday emergencies: families with young children and older people.
To ensure the updated advice is relevant and accessible to all, the ‘Be Ready’ campaign has been built in collaboration with charities and campaigners that work with groups that are often under-represented, including people with insecure housing and people who use foodbanks.
Many of the simple steps are quick and cost-free, like signing up to the Priority Services Register, and other steps are designed to be as low-cost as possible. The intention is that, if households that can take these steps do, emergency services will be able to prioritise those most in-need if an emergency were to happen.
The Government has published resilience advice for households since May 2024. While the ‘Be Ready’ campaign has seen the previous “Prepare” website updated with new messaging and branding, much of the advice has not changed and remains evergreen for households to follow.
Laura Scott, British Red Cross Director for UK Resilience, said:
We can’t control when emergencies happen, but we can all take some simple steps to be prepared, so that when they do, we are ready to help our friends, families and neighbours.
We know from our work across the UK that local people know their communities best and want to play a part when a crisis happens. Having clear and trusted advice for people, especially those who may be more at-risk, could help reduce the impact of crises and even save lives.
